title: Weekly Briefing: Anthropic Researcher Quits Over AI Fears, AI Creates 1 Million Jobs, and U.S. Student Scores Hit New Lows d-education-crisis
author: Future Ready Leadership
summary: This weekly briefing deliberately juxtaposes three stories that at first look unrelated to argue they're all versions of the same underlying question for leaders: are we preparing people and organizations for the technology we're racing to build? The first story — Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's public resignation and warning that AI labs are 'gambling with our lives' — gets a measured response rather than alarm: the author takes technical experts' concerns seriously while pushing back on the leap from 'we can't predict future AI behavior' to 'AI will decide to kill humanity,' pointing instead to concrete, non-sci-fi risks like cyberattacks and misuse. The second story flips the usual AI-jobs narrative by citing The Economist's estimate that AI has created roughly 1 million U.S. jobs against about 200,000 AI-attributed layoffs since 2023, much of it in unglamorous, physical data-center infrastructure work. The third story is the sharpest: the latest PISA results show American 15-year-olds at historic lows in math and reading (only 65% and 74% reaching baseline proficiency respectively) while China and Singapore pull further ahead — a workforce-pipeline problem the author argues deserves as much leadership attention as AI headlines, since it's the same young people who are supposed to become the engineers and judgment-capable professionals an AI economy needs. The briefing's real argument for leaders is that the alarming AI-safety headline and the reassuring jobs data and the discouraging education data all point the same direction: preparation, not panic or complacency, is the actual leadership task.
points: Models a measured response to AI-doom headlines: take technical experts' concerns seriously without leaping from 'unpredictable' to 'will decide to kill humanity' — focus leadership attention on concrete risks like cyberattacks and misuse instead.

Reframes the AI-jobs narrative with data: The Economist estimates AI has created ~1 million U.S. jobs (much of it physical data-center infrastructure work) against ~200,000 AI-attributed layoffs since 2023.

Surfaces a workforce-pipeline problem hiding behind the AI headlines: the latest PISA results show only 65% of U.S. 15-year-olds reaching baseline math proficiency and 74% in reading, at historic lows, as China and Singapore pull ahead.
Argues all three stories are really one leadership question: are we preparing people and organizations for the technology economy already arriving, not whether AI will eliminate jobs.
quotes: I think the concerns deserve attention, especially when they come from people who understand these systems at a technical level. But I am also cautious about jumping from 'we cannot perfectly predict the behavior of future AI' to 'AI will decide to kill humanity.' Those are very different claims.
The Economist looked at the other side of the ledger and estimates that the AI boom has created roughly 1 million U.S. jobs, compared with around 200,000 layoffs attributed to AI since mid-2023.

The assessment tested more than 760,000 15-year-olds across 91 countries and economies, and the results were not encouraging. Average math, reading, and science scores across advanced economies are at historic lows, while U.S. reading and math performance fell to its lowest levels since the assessment began.

We are simultaneously talking about an economy that needs more engineers, scientists, data specialists, and people capable of exercising judgment alongside AI while the underlying reading and math skills of the future workforce are deteriorating.
These stories look unrelated at first, but they are really asking the same question, are we preparing people and organizations for the technology we are racing to create?
